name: Lincoln Road
label: Lincoln Road
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/441809093: large area 'Lincoln Road Mall' (924 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Pedestrian shopping mall lined with cafés.

text.description:
Lincoln Road is the pedestrian shopping street of South Beach, a long, car-free mall running east to west between 16th Street and 17th Street. It was a mangrove forest until 1912, when Carl Fisher cleared a strip across the island from the ocean side to Biscayne Bay. In the 1950s the architect Morris Lapidus redesigned it in his Miami Modern ("MiMo") style, with gardens, fountains, shelters and an amphitheatre. It had its grand opening as a pedestrian mall on 28 November 1960, and it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2011.

For photos, the mall gives you a long straight view with cafe tables, palms, shop fronts and people strolling, so the scene has plenty of depth. Street performers and the mix of old and new buildings add variety, and the Lapidus shapes and planted areas make good foreground detail. Walk a little further to find the garden-style western block by Raymond Jungles, a good place for greenery shots. It is a busy place, so allow time to wait for a gap in the crowd, and watch your bag and phone when you stop to compose.
text.geographic_location: Lincoln Road is in South Beach, in the southern part of Miami Beach. The mall runs between 16th Street and 17th Street, from Washington Avenue in the east to Alton Road in the west.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Lincoln Road area of South Beach and head for the pedestrian mall between 16th and 17th Street. Just walk along the street; it is car-free. The phone icon on the map is about 210 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street as you see it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full width of the mall with tables and palms. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out a performer, a shop front or a detail of the planting.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 210 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the street up with the centre so the shop fronts lead the eye down the mall. Keep your phone level, as tilting will bend the vertical lines of the buildings. Put some tables or planters in the foreground for depth, and wait for a gap in the crowd if you want a clear view. For a closer shot, try a side-on view of a garden or fountain area.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the street or a person to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is washing out. If a stranger is clearly the subject, try portrait mode; otherwise stay with the normal photo mode. After dark, night mode helps with the shop and restaurant lights, but hold the phone against something steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the quietest time for clear views of the street. In the late afternoon and evening the mall is livelier and the lights come on, but you will be facing west, towards the low sun, so use the exposure slider.

text.access_note: Lincoln Road Mall is a public pedestrian street, but check the official site before you go if you plan to photograph inside a venue or at an event.
claims_not_in_sources: Facing west from the east part of the street means shooting towards the sun in the late afternoon.
The mall is quieter in the early morning and busier in the late afternoon and evening.
The shops and restaurants are lit after dark.

name: Fontainebleau Miami Beach
label: Fontainebleau
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Collins Avenue' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Collins Avenue nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/447042031: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fontainebleau' (286 m across).

text.description: The Fontainebleau is one of Miami Beach's best-known mid-century hotels, designed by Morris Lapidus and opened in 1954. Its big curved oceanfront wing is the shape everyone remembers, and it is the reason the hotel works so well in a photo. From Collins Avenue you can line the curve up down the street, and it looks best when the building is lit at dusk or after dark. The hotel has a long film history too. It appears in the opening aerial shot after the credits of the 1964 James Bond film Goldfinger. Its architecture has also been recognised: in 2012 the American Institute of Architects' Florida Chapter ranked it first on its list of Florida's 100 places, and it joined the National Register of Historic Places in December 2008. That was the same year it reopened after a renovation of about $1 billion, which added newer towers while keeping Lapidus's original look. For a phone photo, stand on the pavement of Collins Avenue and look north, so the curved front sits to your right and leads the eye down the avenue. Keep the vertical lines straight with the gridlines. Wait for the lights to come on rather than shooting in flat daylight. An alternative is the hotel's Ocean Lawn on the oceanfront side, which gives sunrise light with the Atlantic in front, but it is hotel property.
text.geographic_location: The Fontainebleau sits on Collins Avenue in Miami Beach, Florida, on the oceanfront side of the avenue.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so head for Collins Avenue in Miami Beach by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Fontainebleau. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the curved facade down the avenue. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the street and sky, but keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can stretch. The telephoto (2x or more) is useful for picking out the curve of the front from further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Collins Avenue (looking north along Collins Avenue toward the curved oceanfront facade). The hotel's curved Lapidus facade framed down the avenue, most striking when the building is lit at night. The hotel's long curved oceanfront front is to the east, on your right, and should lead into the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the avenue's edge as a guide line, keeping the building's verticals upright. Leave some dark sky above the roofline. If you have time at the Ocean Lawn on the oceanfront side, it gives a different view of the building with the sea and sunrise in front, but it is hotel property, so check the official site before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Use night mode once the light drops, and hold the phone steady with your elbows tucked in. Tap on the lit facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights do not wash out. Take a few shots, as passing traffic will change each one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Night, at blue hour, when the facade is lit and the sky still has some colour.

text.access_note: Collins Avenue is a public street, but the hotel and its Ocean Lawn are private property where you may be asked to move on, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ocean Drive
label: Ocean Drive
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18543682: large area 'Ocean Drive' (2276 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Art Deco hotels and neon lights facing the beach.

text.description: Ocean Drive is a major street in South Beach, the southern part of Miami Beach. It runs north from South Pointe, just south of 1st Street, up to 15th Street, close to the Atlantic. It sits at the centre of the Miami Art Deco District, which has about 900 preserved buildings and is on the National Register of Historic Places. The street was developed in the 1920s and 1930s, and the rounded Streamline Moderne style dominates it. That is what you are photographing: rows of pastel hotel fronts, curved corners, neon signs and café terraces, all lined up along one straight street. The 1939 Colony Hotel is described as the most photographed Art Deco hotel here, and it makes an easy anchor for a picture. The Carlyle appeared in The Birdcage (1996), and the Clevelander is another popular Art Deco hotel. The street is long, so pick one stretch and keep your picture simple. A wide shot down the pavement shows the whole line of buildings, while a closer shot of a single sign, balcony or doorway shows the detail. Pavements and terraces get busy, so look for gaps between people or include them for a sense of life.
text.geographic_location: Ocean Drive is in the South Beach district at the southern end of Miami Beach. It runs from South Pointe to 15th Street, starting about a quarter mile west of the Atlantic at its southern end, and lies just south-east of Lincoln Road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. From it, the subject point is about 6 to 7 minutes on foot to the south along the street. The phone icon on the map is about 510 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for most street views. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want a whole hotel front, or when you are close to a building. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a sign or rooftop detail further down the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 510 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. From there the line of Art Deco buildings leads your eye down the road. Walk south for closer pictures of individual hotels.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the buildings straight. Place the street along a diagonal to give the picture depth. For a single hotel, stand square-on to the front and use the 1x lens. For a more relaxed street scene, include a few pedestrians or café tables for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a pastel wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the colours stay rich and neon signs do not blow out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows against something firm to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, with softer light on the facades. Around dusk and after dark the neon signs come on and the street looks quite different.

text.access_note: Ocean Drive is a public street with hotels, bars and restaurants along it; cars were banned during 2020 to 2022 but it has since reopened to traffic, so check the official site before you go for any current changes.

name: Eden Roc Miami Beach Hotel
label: Eden Roc Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Collins Avenue' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Collins Avenue nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/135296603: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Eden Roc Resort Miami Beach' (207 m across).

text.description:
The Eden Roc is a big resort hotel on Collins Avenue in Mid-Beach, designed by Morris Lapidus in the Miami Modern style and finished in 1955–56. Lapidus built it just north of his own Fontainebleau, and the two hotels had a famously bitter rivalry. Where the Fontainebleau is all sweeping curves, the Eden Roc is more formal. The roofline carries a large finned enclosure with the hotel's signs, which is what you want in your frame. A newer 21-story Ocean Tower was added in 2008, and part of the building now operates as the Nobu Hotel Miami Beach.

From the street the hotel is at its best after dark, when the tower is lit and sits in a line with the neighbouring Mid-Beach hotels along Collins Avenue. That gives you a strong, simple picture: glowing vertical shapes against a deep evening sky, with palm trees and car light trails at the bottom of the frame if you want some life in it. Pick a stretch of pavement where nothing blocks the tower, and take a few frames as you walk along rather than settling on the first one. If you would like a softer daytime picture, the hotel's oceanfront side has the tower framed against the beach in morning light, but check the official site before you go to see whether visitors can use the grounds.
text.geographic_location: The Eden Roc is at 4525 Collins Avenue in the Mid-Beach part of Miami Beach, on the ocean side of the avenue and immediately north of the Fontainebleau hotel.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed near this spot. Collins Avenue is the road to follow in Mid-Beach. Check the map to confirm exactly where the point sits, then move around nearby until the tower is clear in your view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) and step back to a point where you can fit the tower in. If the tower is cut off at the top, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out the finned sign structure on the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Collins Avenue (Mid-Beach stretch of Collins Avenue at the hotel). The illuminated Eden Roc tower in a row with the neighbouring Mid-Beach hotels at night. Because this is an area rather than a single exact spot, move a little along the street until the tower is in the frame without trees or signs in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it does not lean. Hold the phone level and keep the tower to one side with the other hotels leading off along the row. If you have time and the grounds are open to visitors, the hotel's oceanfront side makes a good alternative, with the tower framed against the beach in soft morning light.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Use night mode and brace your elbows against your body, or lean on a wall, to keep the picture steady. Tap on the lit tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the signs and windows do not turn into white blobs.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Night, once the hotels are lit. Morning is better for the beach side of the hotel.

text.access_note: Collins Avenue is an ordinary public street, but the hotel's beachfront grounds may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: New World Center
label: New World Center
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Washington Avenue and 17th Street' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Washington Avenue and 17th Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/277037894: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'New World Center' (103 m across).
notes: Frank Gehry concert hall with outdoor projection wall.

text.description:
The New World Center is a concert hall in South Beach, designed by Frank Gehry and opened in January 2011. It is home to the New World Symphony and seats 756 people. From the street it looks calmer than many of Gehry's buildings. The glass-and-white-plaster outside is mostly rectangular, chosen to sit comfortably with Miami Beach's plaster-and-glass look. The curved shapes are kept for the atrium inside. That plain, pale front works well for a phone photo because the lines are clean and the shapes are easy to read.

In front of it is a 2.5-acre public park, with the SoundScape lawn facing a large projection wall. Free 'wallcasts' of concerts and video art are shown on the wall. It is said to be the largest permanently installed projection surface in North America. The building stands one block north of Lincoln Road.

The best frame is the corner of Washington Avenue and 17th Street. From there the building's front and the park lawn fit in one picture. Use the lawn as a foreground, so the photo shows the building in its setting rather than just a wall. After dark the wall can show video projections, which makes an evening shot more colourful. Events can change what is on the lawn, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the South Beach part of Miami Beach, one block north of Lincoln Road. The building looks onto SoundScape Park, a public park beside it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is given for this spot, so head for the Lincoln Road area of South Beach, or come by taxi or hired scooter. The New World Center is one block north of Lincoln Road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole lawn and the building in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Washington Avenue and 17th Street (corner facing the building's front). The New World Center facade across the SoundScape park lawn, with the building and park in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building's vertical edges parallel to the grid lines so they don't lean. Leave a band of lawn at the bottom of the frame. For a different view, walk into SoundScape Park and photograph the lobby's glass front and curved entrance with the landscaping in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building's pale wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the white plaster keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a railing or your body to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go after dark if you want the projections that can appear on the wall, and check the programme for wallcast evenings. By day, the plain facade also photographs cleanly.

text.access_note: The park is a public space, but events or closures may affect it, so check the official site before you go.

name: Casa Casuarina
label: Versace Mansion
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ocean Drive' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Ocean Drive nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/380875533: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Villa Casa Casuarina' (45 m across).
notes: Former Versace home on Ocean Drive.

text.description:
Casa Casuarina, also known as the Versace Mansion, is a Mediterranean Revival house on Ocean Drive in South Beach. It was built in 1930 for Alden Freeman, a wealthy philanthropist, and Freeman said it was modelled on the Alcázar de Colón. The walls carry about 100 medallions of historical figures, and the design includes an observatory and a small tower. Fashion designer Gianni Versace lived here from 1992 until 1997. Since 2015 it has run as a luxury hotel called The Villa Casa Casuarina.

It photographs well because the old stone, ornate entrance and gates stand out against the plainer Ocean Drive frontage. The best picture is the street facade with the gates, taken from the public sidewalk. The property does not allow photography on its grounds, so stay on the pavement and don't step through the gates. The gates are sometimes closed, which hides most of the house, so try to arrive when they are open. If people are in the shot, wait for a gap. A quieter alternative is a partly framed view of the rooftop observatory through a gap in the trees in the park opposite.
text.geographic_location: Casa Casuarina is at 1116 Ocean Drive in the South Beach district of Miami Beach, between 11th and 12th streets. It lies within the Miami Beach Architectural District.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from the South Beach area and go by taxi or hired scooter to Ocean Drive, between 11th and 12th streets. The house is on the west side of the street, with the park and beach on the other side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and gates. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the sidewalk is narrow or busy and you can't step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the stonework, the medallions or the rooftop observatory.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ocean Drive (west side, public sidewalk in front of the mansion's gates, between 11th and 12th streets). The mansion's street facade and entrance gates, framed by the Ocean Drive sidewalk, with the house as the main subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the gates and entrance in the centre, with the house as the main subject. Keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. Wait for people to pass, or include one or two for scale. For a second shot, zoom in on the rooftop observatory framed by the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the house to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if bright light washes out the facade. Avoid portrait mode here, as it can blur the gate bars oddly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the gates are open.

text.access_note: The sidewalk on Ocean Drive is public, but the house is a private hotel that does not allow photography on its grounds, so check the official site before you go if you want to visit.

name: Joe's Stone Crab
label: Joe's Stone Crab
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q6208236: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Joe's Stone Crab is one of the best-known restaurants in Miami Beach, and its long history makes it a good subject for a street-level photo. The story starts in 1913, when Joe Weiss came to Miami Beach for his asthma and the family opened a seafood concession at Smith's Bathing Casino. In 1918 they bought a small house across the street, and Joe's Diner opened there in 1920. Stone crabs went on the menu after a visiting scientist suggested them, and business grew with the tourists. The restaurant became a Miami Beach historic landmark in 1975 and is still run by the family. Fresh claws are served from 15 October to 1 May, which is the legal catch period.

For a phone photo, the aim is to show the building, its entrance and its sign together, with a little street around them to give a sense of place. Keep the camera level and use the gridlines so the walls stay straight. Photographing the outside is the easy part. If you want to go in, or take photos inside, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Joe's Stone Crab is in Miami Beach, Florida.
text.directions_text: From there the restaurant is about 78 m to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole frontage. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the pavement is too narrow to step back, and keep the building centred so the edges don't stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Pick a spot with a clear, open view of the subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line a vertical edge of the building up with a grid line. Leave a strip of pavement or street at the bottom to show the setting. For a closer shot of the sign or doorway, use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) rather than walking into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the facade keeps its colour. If the sign is lit after dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday. After dusk the lit sign can make a good night-mode photo.

text.access_note: The outside can be seen from the public street, but the restaurant is a business, so check the official site before you go for access and any rules on photography inside.

name: Delano Miami Beach Hotel
label: Delano Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Collins Avenue' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Collins Avenue nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/263592326: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Delano South Beach' (71 m across).
notes: Iconic white tower hotel on Collins Avenue.

text.description:
The Delano is a tall white Art Deco-style hotel on the beach side of South Beach, and its slim tower is easy to spot from the street. Architect B. Robert Swartburg designed it, and it opened on 15 December 1948. It has 14 storeys plus a 35-foot tower, which made it one of the tallest and earliest of Miami Beach's postwar MiMo hotels. It is named after President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Designer Philippe Starck led the 1994 renovation, and in 2007 the hotel appeared on the American Institute of Architects' list of "America's Favorite Architecture". It closed in March 2020 and reopened in June 2026 after a redevelopment.

The best phone photo is taken from Collins Avenue, on the block in front of the hotel. From here you can look along the strip, with the hotel's towers rising above neighbouring pastel Art Deco hotels and the everyday street life. Guides describe this stretch as less crowded and full of detail, and they recommend a wide view. If you want the hotel on its own, step back and frame the facade and tower, including the sharp corners and the winged column that gives the hotel its look. Tall hedges can hide much of the building from the pavement, and renovation work may affect the view, so be ready to shoot at an angle or concentrate on the tower. Check that the hotel is open and in its current state before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Delano is in South Beach, in the Art Deco part of Miami Beach, directly on the beach.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot. Walk along the block in front of the hotel to find a gap in the hedges and a clear view up to the tower. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the hotel strip and the street. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the hotel. Use 2x or the telephoto lens, if your phone has one, to pick out the tower and the winged column.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Collins Avenue (the block in front of the hotel, looking along the Art Deco hotel strip). The hotel's towers seen down the street alongside neighbouring pastel Art Deco hotels and the street life of the strip. The hotel is to the east. If you want the facade and tower alone, use the Delano Miami Beach frontage as a second option.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up a vertical edge of the tower with a grid line so the building does not lean. For the street view, include the pavement and neighbouring hotels to show the row of Art Deco buildings. For the facade, find a gap in the hedges or move along the block, and keep the sharp corners and the winged column in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright white facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the walls keep their detail against the sky. Take a few shots at slightly different angles, since hedges or scaffolding may block some of them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun is behind you as you look east at the hotel. Early morning is usually quieter on the street.

text.access_note: The Collins Avenue frontage is a public street, but the hotel itself is a private business, so check the official site before you go for its current status and for any access to the hotel.
claims_not_in_sources: Collins Avenue is the public street on the west side of the hotel, and the hotel lies east of the stand-here point.
Late afternoon sun comes from the west, behind a photographer looking east towards the hotel.
The street is usually quieter in the early morning.
Hotel grounds and interiors are private and may be restricted to guests.

name: Lummus Park
label: Lummus Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ocean Drive at 6th Street' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Ocean Drive and 6th Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/76677464: large area 'Lummus Park' (1391 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Palm-lined beach park with colorful lifeguard towers.

text.description: Lummus Park is the long green strip between Ocean Drive and the beach in South Beach. It covers about 74 acres (30 ha) and is named after the Lummus brothers, two of Miami's early pioneers. The park was redesigned in the mid-1980s as part of the wider revival of the Art Deco district, and it has appeared in television shows such as Miami Vice and Burn Notice. That history helps explain why it looks so good in photos. Lawns and palm trees sit in the foreground, the Atlantic lies behind them, and the Art Deco buildings of Ocean Drive line the other side of the road. A wavy pedestrian Promenade runs between the grass and the sand, which gives you a natural curving line to use in a picture. For the classic view, stand at Ocean Drive at 6th Street, on the west side of Ocean Drive, and look across the road at the park and the ocean. An old 1946 postcard was taken looking south along Ocean Drive, so a shot in that direction has some history behind it. If you want a quieter picture, walk along the park and look for a stretch of lawn and palms with fewer people in it. The colourful Miami Beach sign is another popular spot, but it may be a temporary installation, so check it is still there. The area can be very busy at weekends and in tourist hours, so wait for a gap or choose a tighter framing.
text.geographic_location: Lummus Park is in South Beach, on the ocean side of Ocean Drive between roughly 5th and 15th Streets, next to the Art Deco buildings of Ocean Drive and the beach.
text.directions_text: From there, the middle of the park is about 570 m (a short walk) to the north, along the park and the Promenade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the lawn, palms, ocean and Ocean Drive frontage together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out palm trees or the sign and keep passers-by out of frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Ocean Drive and 6th Street (west side of Ocean Drive, facing the park and the ocean). The park's green lawn and palm trees in the foreground, with the Atlantic and the Art Deco frontage of Ocean Drive framing the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on a lower line, with the palms and lawn filling the bottom of the picture. Include a stretch of the curving Promenade as a lead-in line. For a quieter picture, try a stretch of lawn with fewer people, aimed towards the Ocean Drive buildings. The Miami Beach sign, if it is still in place, also works in front of the lawn and palms.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the sea to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out. Wait for traffic and people to clear, or take a Live Photo and pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer, and weekends and midday are very busy. In the afternoon the sun should be behind you as you face the park and sea.

text.access_note: Lummus Park is a public park, but check the official site before you go for any events or temporary closures.

notes: Waterfront park and pier at the southern tip with cruise ship views.

text.description: South Pointe Park is a 17-acre park at the very southern tip of South Beach, where the Atlantic meets the ship channel at Government Cut. It photographs well because the land opens out in every direction. You get sea, passing ships, the port and the Downtown Miami skyline across the water, with Fisher Island and Biscayne Bay beyond. The park opened on 25 October 1985 and was redesigned by Hargreaves Associates, with the work finished around March 2009. That redesign added the wide limestone-lined walkways, which make easy foreground lines for a phone shot. The best-known spot is South Pointe Pier, about 450 feet long, which makes a natural leading line out over the water. Walk out to the end and you can frame cruise ships gliding through the channel with the downtown skyline behind them. Turn back toward the beach and you catch the South Beach hotels and a lifeguard tower, which works especially well at sunrise. Give yourself time to wander, because the view changes with every few steps along the walkways and the jetty. Ships move steadily, so take a few frames as one passes and pick the best. Keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines, and check the edges of the frame for stray people or bins.
text.geographic_location: South Pointe Park is at the southern end of South Beach, in Miami Beach, with Government Cut and the shipping channel along its southern edge.
text.directions_text: There are no Metro or tram stops to give you, so head to the southern end of South Beach and ask for South Pointe Park or South Pointe Pier. From there, the middle of the park is about 400 m (roughly 5 minutes on foot) to the north-west. Follow the wide walkways and you will not need street directions. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole length of the pier and the sky. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the sea and the hotels. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a cruise ship or the downtown skyline from the end of the pier.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on South Pointe Pier (out on the pier, looking back toward the beach for sunrise; the end of the pier for open views). The pier leads the eye out over the Atlantic, with the South Beach hotels and lifeguard tower behind you at sunrise, or cruise ships and the downtown skyline from the end.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the pier's line as a leading line: turn on gridlines, place the pier along one third of the frame and keep the horizon level. At the end of the pier, wait for a ship to pass through the channel and frame it against the skyline. If you want a different angle, the park's waterside walkways and South Pointe Beach, with the jetty rocks in the foreground, also work for ships in the channel.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or sea to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunrise colours don't wash out. At blue hour, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady. Try a short Live Photo of a ship passing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise is the classic time. Sunset and blue hour are also good, and are easier on the eyes if you're not an early riser.

text.access_note: The park is an open public space, but the pier is generally open from around sunrise to sunset and can close in rough weather, so check the posted hours and the official site before you go.

name: Bass Museum
label: The Bass
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Collins Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Collins Park' (way/76691659): middle (396 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/483322279: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bass Museum of Art' (110 m across).
notes: Contemporary art museum in Collins Park.

text.description:
The Bass is a contemporary art museum in Miami Beach, set beside a public park. Its front is built of coral rock, which gives the building a warm, textured look. From across the lawn you can fit the whole frontage into one picture, with palm trees on either side and the park's pond in the foreground. The Sylvie Fleury sculpture Eternity Now is also in view, which adds a splash of modern art to the scene.

The museum opened in 1964 in a building that had once been the Miami Beach Public Library. It was extended in 2002 with a wing designed by Arata Isozaki, and a further expansion by David Gauld reopened in 2017. Two outdoor works were acquired together in 2016 under the museum's new public-art initiative: Eternity Now by Sylvie Fleury, which dates from 2015, and Miami Mountain by Ugo Rondinone, which dates from 2016.

For your photo, stay back on the grass rather than walking up to the doors. The distance lets the building sit inside its green surroundings. Look for a clear gap between the palms so none of them cut across the facade. If you want a second picture, Miami Mountain, the five stacked, brightly coloured boulders, makes a bold foreground with the museum behind it. Photography rules inside the galleries can differ from the outdoor views, so ask staff if you want to shoot inside.
text.geographic_location: The Bass Museum is in the Collins Park area of Miami Beach, at 2100 Collins Avenue. The park lies in front of the museum, between the building and the ocean.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or similar stop at this spot, so head for Collins Park in Miami Beach. From there the museum is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front of the museum with the palms and pond. If the lawn is crowded and you cannot step back far enough, the ultra-wide (0.5x) fits more in, but keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched. Use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out the coral-rock texture or the Sylvie Fleury sculpture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Collins Park (across the lawn from the main entrance). The museum's coral-rock front framed by palm trees and the park's pond, with the Sylvie Fleury sculpture Eternity Now in view. The museum is to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the building's front along the upper or lower third line, with the pond or lawn filling the rest. Let a palm trunk or fronds frame one side, and keep the verticals of the building straight by holding the phone level. For a different shot, Miami Mountain is a good alternative: the colourful boulders go in the foreground, with the museum building behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the coral-rock front to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building stays rich in colour. Try a Live Photo if people or palm fronds are moving, so you can choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the light falls well on the coral rock.

text.access_note: Collins Park is a public green space and the outdoor views can be photographed from it, but check the official site before you go if you plan to visit the museum itself.

name: Española Way
label: Española Way
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-16: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).

text.description:
Española Way sits in South Beach, the part of Miami Beach south of Dade Boulevard and the first section of the city to be developed, from the 1910s onwards. It is a good place to slow down with your phone. The street is narrow and walkable, with low buildings, painted walls, café tables and signs that give you plenty of colour and depth, so you can take wide scene-setting shots and close-ups in the same few minutes.

It also belongs to a bigger story. In the 1930s South Beach filled with Art Deco, Streamline Moderne and Nautical Moderne buildings, and almost one square mile of the area was protected as the Miami Beach Architectural District in 1979. Española Way is part of that wider neighbourhood, so it is worth lifting your eyes to rooflines, signs and window details as well as shooting at street level.

For photographs, think in layers. Put something in the foreground, such as a café chair, a lamp or a doorway, and let the street lead the eye towards the far end. Keep your phone upright for the long view along the street, and turn it sideways for details and for groups of people. Keep the gridlines on so the buildings stay straight. Be patient: people walk through constantly, which can add life to a frame, and a few seconds' wait often gives you a clear one.
text.geographic_location: Española Way is in South Beach, the southern part of Miami Beach, between Biscayne Bay and the Atlantic Ocean.
text.directions_text: The phone icon on the map is about 1.4 km north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for natural-looking street views. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole narrow street in one frame, and to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for signs, window details and compressed views along the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 1.4 km north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Then stand at one end of the street and shoot along it, keeping the buildings on both sides in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn gridlines on and line up the building edges with the vertical lines. Put a chair, lamp or doorway in the foreground, and let the street lead the eye to the far end. Use portrait mode for a person or a café detail against a softly blurred background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the colours stay rich and the sky is not washed out. If people are walking through the frame, try a Live Photo and pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, so you get cleaner views along the street. In the evening, Night mode helps with café lights and signs; hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: This looks like an ordinary street open to walkers, but individual cafés and venues set their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Holocaust Memorial of the Greater Miami Jewish Federation
label: Holocaust Memorial
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Meridian Avenue' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Meridian Avenue and Dade Boulevard (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/92334592: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Holocaust Memorial' (118 m across).
notes: Sculptural memorial with a giant outstretched arm.

text.description:
This memorial in Miami Beach remembers the victims of the Holocaust. It is best known for a very tall bronze arm and hand reaching up from a pool, and you can often see the hand over the greenery from the street before you go in. The memorial was conceived by a committee of survivors in 1984 and designed by Kenneth Treister. It opened on 4 February 1990, with Elie Wiesel as guest speaker at the dedication. The site was once the family home of Holocaust survivors William and Florrie Loeb. A few trees at the back were planted by the original owners in the 1920s and 1930s.

For photographs, the street corner on Meridian Avenue gives a clear view of the sculpture's full height against the sky, with greenery around it. If you go inside, the bronze arm and hand rising from the water can be framed through the openings of the tunnel, with the figures in the foreground. The Miami Beach Botanical Garden is a quieter, wider viewpoint of the whole memorial set among plants. Start at the street corner, then decide how much more you want to take once you are inside.

This is a solemn place, so keep your phone use quiet and respectful, and avoid posed or playful pictures. Photography is generally allowed for personal use, but check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The memorial is at 1933-1945 Meridian Avenue in Miami Beach, at the corner of Meridian Avenue and Dade Boulevard.
text.directions_text: Head for Meridian Avenue at Dade Boulevard in Miami Beach; there is no station or tram stop for this spot. From there the centre of the memorial is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from the street for the full height of the hand. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) inside if you want the tunnel and the figures in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the hand and fingers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Meridian Avenue and Dade Boulevard (corner at the memorial's street frontage). The tall outstretched hand seen from the street, rising above the surrounding greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and hold the phone upright (portrait) so the hand fills the height of the frame, with a little greenery at the bottom. Keep the sky as clean background above the fingertips. As an alternative, inside the memorial try the bronze arm and hand rising from the water, seen through the tunnel openings with the figures in front. The Miami Beach Botanical Garden gives a softer, wider view of the whole complex.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hand to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bronze keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white. Skip portrait mode here; it works best on people, not on a large sculpture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the bronze. Check the opening times first, as they may differ from what you expect.

text.access_note: The street view of the hand is from a public road, but opening hours and any admission rules for the memorial itself can vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Wolfsonian–FIU
label: The Wolfsonian
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '10th Street & Washington Avenue' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Washington Avenue and 10th Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/449002308: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Wolfsonian - FIU' (50 m across).
notes: Design museum in a Mediterranean Revival building.

text.description: The Wolfsonian–FIU sits in the heart of Miami Beach's Art Deco District. It is a museum, library and research centre, and it works well as a photo stop because the building stands on a street corner, so you can see its Mediterranean Revival facade in one frame with the everyday street life around it. The building began as the Washington Storage Company facility, which had been operating since 1926. Collector Mitchell Wolfson Jr. stored his growing collection there, bought the building in 1986, and had it converted into a museum that opened to the public in 1995. In 1997 it became part of Florida International University. Inside are roughly 180,000 pieces dated 1885 to 1945, including furniture, glass, ceramics, rare books and works on paper. For a phone photo, the exterior is the easiest subject. Stand back at the corner so the whole facade fits, and keep the camera level so the vertical lines stay straight. Traffic and parked vehicles can get in the way, so wait for a gap, or move a few steps along the pavement. For a closer shot, the entrance and gate on Washington Avenue make a neat second picture, with the facade behind them. Check the official site for visiting arrangements before you go, as the museum may have limited days.
text.geographic_location: The Wolfsonian–FIU is in the Art Deco District of Miami Beach, on the corner of 10th Street and Washington Avenue.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Art Deco District in Miami Beach and head for the corner of 10th Street and Washington Avenue. The museum's corner facade is easy to recognise once you are there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole corner facade in from the pavement. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the entrance and decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Washington Avenue and 10th Street (the corner where the museum's Mediterranean Revival facade faces the street). The whole corner facade of the 1927 former storage building, framed by the Art Deco district's street traffic and sidewalks. From here you can photograph the whole corner facade with the Art Deco district's traffic and pavements around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them, so it doesn't look as if it is leaning. Keep the whole corner in the frame and include a little street for context. If you want a closer, tighter picture, 1001 Washington Avenue shows the entrance and gate at close range, with the facade behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its colour and detail. If cars pass through the shot, a Live Photo can help you pick a clear frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day is likely to give softer light and quieter pavements, but any time works for the exterior.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public street, but going inside is a museum visit, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
Miami Beach Community Church is a church building in Miami Beach, and it makes a calm, quiet subject among the busier sights on the map. This is a simple, practical spot rather than a showpiece. A photo of a church works well when you show the whole building and a little of its surroundings, so the picture says 'this is a real neighbourhood landmark' and not just 'a building'.

The phone icon on the map is about 70 m north-east of the subject. That gap is helpful. You can see the whole building without tilting the phone upwards, which keeps the walls looking straight. Start with the default lens (1x) and turn on the gridlines, so the vertical edges of the building line up with the vertical lines on the screen. If you want the building to fill more of the picture, try 2x or 3x if your phone has a telephoto lens. This also helps to leave out clutter such as parked cars and signs.

Wait a moment for people and vehicles to pass before you take the shot. Take one wide picture that shows the setting and one closer picture of the entrance or a detail that catches your eye. I can't give you any history, dates or measurements for this church here, so check the church's own website or noticeboard if you want to know more. If you plan to go inside, check the official site before you go, as visiting arrangements can change.
text.geographic_location: Miami Beach Community Church is in Miami Beach, Florida.
text.directions_text: From there the church is 71 m to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot. Follow the map for the last part of the way. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building and its setting. Use 2x or 3x on a telephoto phone to fill the frame and cut out street clutter. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk closer and can't fit the building in, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the building with the vertical grid lines. Leave a little space around the church so it looks as if it belongs to its street. Take a second, tighter shot of the entrance or a detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church on the screen to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour and detail. Take a few frames while cars and people pass.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is a good bet, because the sun should be behind you as you face the church. Late afternoon can also look good, but you may be shooting towards the sun, so check the screen and lower the exposure if needed.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship and may have set visiting times or rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Miami Beach Architectural District
label: Art Deco District
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Colony Hotel' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Colony Hotel' (way/435587753): middle (44 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3307877: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: World-famous cluster of pastel Art Deco buildings.

text.description: The Miami Beach Architectural District, often called the Miami Art Deco District, is an area of South Beach with 960 historic buildings. It was designated a historic district on 14 May 1979 and holds what is described as the largest collection of Art Deco buildings in the world. Most were built between the Great Depression and the early 1940s, after the real estate slump of 1925 and the 1926 hurricane. The district runs from the Atlantic Ocean in the east to Alton Road in the west, and from Sixth Street up to the Collins Canal and Dade Boulevard. It photographs well because the buildings are low, colourful and easy to fit in a frame, with palm trees and the beach right beside them. For a phone photo, start at The Colony Hotel at 736 Ocean Drive, at the southern end of the main Ocean Drive run. Its pastel Art Deco front, symmetrical layout and blue neon sign make it the building most often pictured in the district. The Ocean Drive hotels run from 5th to 15th Streets and face Lummus Park, so you can also step back into the park for a wider view of the whole row. For something softer, Española Way has pink Mediterranean Revival façades with tiled roofs and strings of lights. It is a Mediterranean Revival street that some records list within the district, though it is not Art Deco. Early morning or sunset gives the nicest colour, and the street is at its busiest at night.
text.geographic_location: In the South Beach neighbourhood of Miami Beach, between the Atlantic Ocean and Alton Road. The most photographed stretch is Ocean Drive, facing Lummus Park and the beach.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot; check local transport options for reaching South Beach and Ocean Drive. The middle of the district, as marked on the map, is about 955 m (roughly 12 minutes on foot) to the north of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the hotel front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is crowded or you want more of the street. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the neon sign and the Art Deco details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at The Colony Hotel (front façade on Ocean Drive at 736 Ocean Drive, shot from the sidewalk across the street). The pastel Art Deco façade with its symmetrical layout and blue neon sign, the hotel most often pictured in the district. The rest of the district stretches away to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the hotel's centre up with the middle of the frame, since the façade is symmetrical. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. For a wider view of the whole row of façades with palms and beach, walk into Lummus Park. Española Way is a quieter option with pink buildings and strings of lights.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hotel front to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the neon keeps its colour and the sky is not washed out. At dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or sunset. Ocean Drive is busiest at night.

text.access_note: The Colony Hotel front and Lummus Park can be photographed from public pavement and parkland, but check the official site before you go for any access rules.

name: The Tides (Miami Beach)
label: The Tides
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lummus Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lummus Park' (way/76677464): edge nearest the subject (1383 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7769217: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Landmark Art Deco hotel on Ocean Drive.

text.description:
The Tides is an Art Deco building on Ocean Drive in South Beach. It has 11 storeys and stands 49 metres tall. When it was finished in 1936 it was the tallest building in Miami Beach and one of the tallest in Florida. It was renovated in 1997 and is now a residential condominium and luxury hotel, currently known as the King & Grove Tides South Beach.

It photographs well because of its clean, stepped, vertical shape. It rises above the low buildings and palm trees around it, so even a simple phone shot has a clear subject. The best view is from Lummus Park, the green strip across Ocean Drive on the beach side. From there you look back over the palms to the row of Art Deco fronts along the street, with The Tides among them. For a second, closer picture, walk onto Ocean Drive itself. There you can catch the hotel's facade at street level, with the neon-lit strip and palm trees around it.

Keep the tall tower in mind when you frame the shot: it is much taller than its neighbours, so leave room above it. Cars, scooters and pedestrians are often in the way on the street, so take a few frames and pick the cleanest. The hotel's address is 1220 Ocean Drive. Please check that it is operating before you plan a visit, and check the official site if you want to go inside.
text.geographic_location: The Tides is on Ocean Drive in South Beach, in the south of Miami Beach. It sits among the Art Deco hotels in the row facing Lummus Park and the beach.
text.directions_text: Start from South Beach, the Ocean Drive area, and come by taxi or hired scooter. Head for Lummus Park on the beach side of Ocean Drive, opposite 1220 Ocean Drive. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the palms and the Art Deco row. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick The Tides out from its neighbours.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lummus Park (Across Ocean Drive from the hotel, on the beach side of the street). A wide-angle view back across the palms toward the Art Deco frontage of Ocean Drive, with The Tides among the buildings in the row.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the palms in the foreground and let the Art Deco row run across the frame, with The Tides as the tallest shape in it. Turn on gridlines and keep the tower upright against the vertical lines, with space above its top. For a different picture, walk to Ocean Drive and shoot the hotel's facade at street level, framed by the neon and the palm trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hotel to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the pale walls keep their detail. Use the gridlines to keep the verticals straight, and take a few frames so you have one without traffic or people in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try the morning, when the sun may light the front of the building. Go early if you want fewer people on the street.

text.access_note: Lummus Park and Ocean Drive are public outdoor spaces, but the hotel is a private business, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

label: Colony Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lincoln Road' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Lincoln Road and Lenox Avenue (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q97474319: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Art Deco theatre on Lincoln Road.

text.description:
The Colony Theatre is a small Art Deco theatre on Lincoln Road in Miami Beach. Paramount Pictures opened it in 1935 as a movie house with 1,200 seats, and it was once nicknamed the "Beauty Queen". Over the years it swapped between cinema and live shows. In 2006 the city carried out a major renovation to bring back its original Art Deco look. Today it is a 417-seat venue run by the theatre company Miami New Drama.

It photographs well because the building has a clear, symmetrical front and a lit marquee, which guides describe as its signature feature. The best view is head-on from that point. A second option is to stand further back along Lincoln Road and shoot towards the theatre, so the street leads your eye to the facade.

Lincoln Road is a busy pedestrian street, so expect people walking through your shot. Wait a moment for a gap, or include a few passers-by to show the street's atmosphere. The evening is the most rewarding time, when the marquee is lit. Photography inside during shows is generally not permitted, but the exterior is fine.
text.geographic_location: The Colony Theatre stands on Lincoln Road in Miami Beach, on the busy pedestrian stretch of the street. The entrance sits on a diagonal corner facing the marquee.
text.directions_text: Head for Lincoln Road in Miami Beach. Once you are on Lincoln Road, look for the theatre's marquee and diagonal corner entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural look at the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if pedestrians or the pavement edge stop you stepping back far enough to fit the whole front in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Lincoln Road and Lenox Avenue (diagonal corner entrance, facing the marquee). The Art Deco facade, ticket box area and lit marquee of the theatre head-on from the corner where its entrance sits. Face south-east towards the diagonal corner entrance and marquee.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the marquee in the centre of the frame, with the building's vertical edges following the grid lines. Hold the phone level to avoid leaning walls. For a different view, walk back along Lincoln Road and photograph the theatre at the end of the street, using the pedestrian street as a leading line.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the marquee to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lit sign doesn't wash out into white. If the light is low, night mode can help, but hold the phone steady for the extra second or two.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the marquee is lit; one guide calls it especially lively for an evening shoot.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public street, but photography inside during shows is generally not allowed, so check the official site before you go for performances or visits.

text.description:
The Warsaw Ballroom was a gay nightclub in South Beach, at Collins Avenue and Espanola Way. Under that name it began as a dance club for seniors. It then changed hands and became the Ovo and the China Club, before returning to the Warsaw name as a gay club. In 1989 Andrew Delaplaine took over the lease and renamed it the Warsaw Ballroom, and David Padilla was offered the resident DJ spot around the same time. The club closed in 1999 and Jerry's Famous Deli took its place.

This is a spot for a street-corner photo with a story behind it, rather than a grand view. It works well as a record of a piece of South Beach nightlife history, set among the buildings and street life of the Collins Avenue and Espanola Way junction. Look for the corner shape of the building, the shopfront and the signs, and let the passers-by add some life to the frame.

Keep it simple. Take one wider shot to show the corner and its surroundings, then a closer one of the shopfront or signage. Wait a moment for people to clear the pavement, or let a few walk through for scale. Check the exact frontage on the day, as businesses here can change their signs and layouts.
text.geographic_location: In South Beach, in the southern part of Miami Beach, on the corner where Collins Avenue meets Espanola Way.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot, so start from the South Beach area around Collins Avenue and Espanola Way. If you are coming from elsewhere in Miami Beach, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the corner of Collins Avenue and Espanola Way. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the corner. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole frontage in. Use telephoto (2x) for details such as signs or the upper part of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. This keeps you close enough to fill the frame with the corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edge of the building with a vertical line so the walls do not lean. Keep the shopfront in the lower half and leave some sky above. For a second shot, step in and frame just the sign and entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. If you use the ultra-wide, keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means quieter pavements. Late afternoon can give warmer light, but check how the sun falls on the frontage when you arrive.

text.access_note: The building is seen from the street; Jerry's Famous Deli replaced the club in 1999, so check what is there now before you go.
